opus-5.5.text:
Working with Fei-Fei has been really eye-opening for me, and I think the biggest change is in how I frame the problems I work on.

For a long time my work sat in a fairly classic part of computer vision: architectures, representation learning, things like ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, diffusion transformers. That work is mostly about building better tools. Fei-Fei pushes you to step back and ask a more fundamental question: what is vision actually *for*? For her, vision isn't just labeling pixels or generating pretty images. It's the foundation of intelligence. It's how animals, and eventually machines, understand and act in a three-dimensional world.

That's where our collaboration on spatial intelligence came from. In the "Thinking in Space" work, we asked a simple-sounding question: today's multimodal large language models can chat about images and videos fluently, but do they actually understand space? Can they remember where things are in a room, estimate distances and sizes, and reason about layouts the way a person walking through a house would? We built a benchmark around that, and the answer was largely no. The models are very good at linguistic shortcuts but quite weak at building something like a cognitive map. That result made me rethink a lot of assumptions about where the field is heading.

The second thing she's expanded for me is the time horizon. Fei-Fei has a historian's sense of the field. She'll connect what we're doing now to the Cambrian explosion, to the history of psychology, to ImageNet and how a data problem became a scientific one. That makes you more willing to work on things that look unfashionable in the short term but matter over ten years. Right now there's huge pressure for everything to be about language models. She gives you the confidence to say that language is only one part of intelligence, and that the physical, spatial, visual world is just as important, maybe more fundamental.

Finally, there's a human side. She cares about the people and the purpose behind the research, not just the leaderboard numbers. Seeing someone at her level stay that curious and that principled has influenced how I think about running my own lab and mentoring students. So the boundaries she's expanded aren't only technical. They're about what kind of researcher I want to be.

r001.rationale: The response describes studying spatial understanding in image and video models, but does not identify deciding which problems matter in video understanding as a research focus.

fable-5.1.text:
Working with Fei-Fei has changed how I think about what a research problem even is. I came up through the architecture side of computer vision, designing networks, scaling them, measuring things on benchmarks. That work trains you to ask very precise, very local questions: does this block help, does this loss help, how does it scale. Fei-Fei asks a different kind of question. She asks what intelligence is for, what seeing is for, and she keeps pulling the conversation back to the agent that has to live in a world and act in it.

The concrete place this shows up for me is spatial intelligence. For years I was content to say that if you train a model on enough images and language, understanding of the physical world will fall out. Fei-Fei pushed me to notice how much is still missing. These models can describe a photo beautifully and still not know where things are, how far apart they sit, what happens if you move the camera a meter to the left. That gap went from being a footnote in my head to being the main thing I want to work on, and I don't think I would have gotten there on my own.

The other thing she expanded is my sense of time horizon. ImageNet took years before anyone appreciated it, and she talks about that very plainly, as a decision to build infrastructure for a question rather than chase the result of the quarter. In an era where the field moves week to week, having someone next to you who is comfortable betting on a five or ten year arc is genuinely freeing. It gives you permission to work on things that aren't fashionable yet.

And honestly, there is a human dimension. She cares a lot about who gets to do this work and what it does to people. I came in thinking of that as something separate from the science. I now think the two are tangled together, and that has changed which problems I pick and how I run my own group.

r001.rationale: The response describes how collaboration shifted Xie toward spatial intelligence and broader questions about which problems to pursue, but it does not identify video understanding as the focus.

astra-6.text:
Working with Fei-Fei has encouraged me to step back from a particular technical problem and ask what larger question we’re trying to answer. In computer vision, it’s easy to focus on improving a model or a benchmark result. That work matters, but so does asking what those improvements actually tell us about visual intelligence.

I’d describe the influence as broadening how I choose problems: thinking about the relationship between data, models, and the world they’re meant to understand, rather than treating each piece in isolation. It’s also a reminder to keep people in the picture—who a system is useful for, and whether the way we evaluate it reflects that purpose.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the collaboration broadened how Xie chooses problems, but does not identify video understanding as the research area.

sol-6.1.text:
Working with Fei-Fei has encouraged me to connect technical questions with a broader question: what would it take for a machine to understand the visual world? It’s easy to focus on a particular architecture or benchmark. That broader perspective pushes you to ask what capabilities are still missing and whether you’re measuring the right things.

It also makes the relationship between data and models especially interesting. When a system struggles, is the limitation in the architecture, the training objective, or the experience we’re giving it? Thinking across those boundaries opens up research directions that you might miss if you treated each component separately.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing meaningful questions and measurements for visual understanding generally, but does not identify determining which problems matter in video understanding as a research focus.
